title: s-Block Elements (Alkali and Alkaline Earth Metals) and Hydrogen
subcategory: The s-Block Elements / Hydrogen — Group 1 and 2 Trends, Diagonal Relationship, Hydrides

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part II, Class 11 — Hydrogen; The s-Block Elements

summary: Alkali metals (group 1) are the most reactive metals with characteristic flame colours; alkaline earth metals (group 2) show similar but generally less pronounced trends; lithium and beryllium (the first members of each group) show a distinctive 'diagonal relationship' with magnesium and aluminium respectively, and hydrogen's unique single-electron structure lets it form three fundamentally different types of hydrides.
explanation: Alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) have a single loosely-held valence electron (ns¹), giving them very LOW ionization enthalpy, high reactivity (react vigorously with water and oxygen), strongly basic hydroxides, and characteristic FLAME TEST colours (Li — crimson red, Na — golden yellow, K — lilac) used for qualitative identification, arising from electronic transitions when the metal's electrons are thermally excited and fall back, emitting light of a specific, element-characteristic wavelength. Alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) have two valence electrons (ns²) and are generally LESS reactive than the corresponding alkali metal in the same period (higher ionization enthalpy due to greater nuclear charge), form less strongly basic hydroxides (basicity increasing down the group, e.g. Mg(OH)₂ is weaker base than Ba(OH)₂), and their solubility/thermal stability trends for carbonates and sulphates typically increase down the group (with some specific exceptions worth noting, like BeSO₄ and MgSO₄ being more soluble than the heavier group members' sulphates). The DIAGONAL RELATIONSHIP describes how certain PERIOD 2 elements (particularly Li and Be) resemble the element diagonally below-and-right in the NEXT period (Mg and Al respectively) more closely than they resemble other members of their OWN group — this arises because diagonal elements often have similar ionic size/charge density despite being in different groups/periods, giving genuinely similar chemical behaviour (e.g., both Li and Mg form a stable nitride directly with N₂, both form covalent-character chlorides, both carbonates decompose on heating relatively easily, unlike the rest of their respective groups). HYDROGEN, despite occupying group 1 in most periodic tables (due to its single electron and +1 oxidation state tendency), is genuinely UNIQUE and doesn't neatly belong to any single group — it forms THREE distinct types of hydrides: IONIC (saline) hydrides with highly electropositive s-block metals (like NaH, CaH₂, containing the H⁻ hydride ion), COVALENT (molecular) hydrides with similarly-or-more-electronegative p-block elements (like CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, HF, sharing electrons), and METALLIC (interstitial) hydrides with many d-block/f-block transition metals (H atoms occupy interstitial spaces in the metal lattice, often giving non-stoichiometric composition and retaining metallic properties like conductivity).
commonMisconceptions: Assuming lithium behaves just like the rest of the alkali metals (Na, K, etc.) — lithium is notably anomalous, showing a diagonal relationship with magnesium instead, differing in reactivity, hydration behaviour, and stability of its compounds.

Believing all alkaline earth metal carbonates/sulphates show identical solubility and thermal stability trends across the whole group — while broad trends exist, specific solubility exceptions (like BeSO₄/MgSO₄ being more soluble than heavier members' sulphates) are frequently tested deviations.

Treating hydrogen as simply belonging to the alkali metal group with fully analogous chemistry — hydrogen's single electron and small size make its chemistry genuinely distinct, capable of forming three fundamentally different hydride types depending on its bonding partner, unlike any true alkali metal.
examples: Sodium metal gives a characteristic golden-yellow flame test colour, while potassium gives a lilac colour, letting these ions be distinguished qualitatively without instrumentation.
Lithium (like magnesium, its diagonal relative) reacts directly with nitrogen gas to form a nitride (Li₃N), a reaction none of the other alkali metals undergo directly under similar conditions.
genZNote: Lithium skipped the alkali metal group chat and started acting like magnesium instead — diagonal relationship energy.
